questions.prompt: Put the six steps of the writing process back in the order you follow them, from the blank page to the finished article.
questions.explanation: You cannot organize ideas you have not generated, so generating ideas comes first and planning and organizing them second. The first draft is written from that plan, and it is the draft — not the plan — that a classmate reads, so sharing and responding follows it. Revising and editing comes next because it works on the marks you have just received: revising changes the content, editing checks spelling, punctuation, grammar and linkers. Only when nothing is left to change do you copy out the final draft and give its format and layout your attention. Content before form, always.

questions.prompt: A classmate has written: "The school has a ramp at its entrance. Therefore, pupils in wheelchairs still cannot reach the first floor." The two sentences contrast, so the link word is wrong. Which symbol of the correction code do you write above "Therefore"?
questions.explanation: The code keeps a symbol of its own for a link word that does not fit the relation between two ideas: W.L, wrong linker. Here the second sentence contradicts the first, so a linker of contrast such as However was needed, not a linker of consequence. V is kept for an ordinary word that does not exist or does not fit the meaning, G for a mistake in a grammatical form, and W.O. for words placed in the wrong order.

questions.prompt: In which of these sentences must the missing verb be in the present perfect rather than the past simple? Select ALL that apply.

options.text: "The headmaster ___ (be) in charge of this school since 2004."
"We ___ (never / have) to cancel an examination before."
"Attendance ___ (fall) by half over the past three weeks."

questions.explanation: "Since 2004" opens a stretch of time that reaches the present, so the sentence takes has been. "Never … before" asks about experience up to today, so it takes have never had. "Over the past three weeks" is a period that includes the present moment, so it takes has fallen. Only "last Monday" names a moment that is over and closed, and a closed moment always takes the past simple: closed.

questions.prompt: On Friday the school nurse told the parents: "We started the vaccinations yesterday, and today we are up to two hundred children." Which sentence reports her words correctly?

options.text: She said that they started the vaccinations yesterday and that today they were up to two hundred children.
She said that they have started the vaccinations the day before and that that day they were up to two hundred children.
She said that they had started the vaccinations the day before and that that day they were up to two hundred children.
She said that they had started the vaccinations the previous day and that that day they are up to two hundred children.

questions.explanation: Reporting after a past verb moves three things at once. The tenses step back: the past simple started becomes the past perfect had started, and the present are becomes were. The time words move away from the moment of speaking: yesterday becomes the day before, today becomes that day. Leaving yesterday and today untouched reports nothing at all; have started steps the tense back but not far enough; and the version that keeps are leaves one verb behind in the present although the other has moved.

questions.prompt: A journalist asked the headmaster: "Where are the sick pupils now?" Which sentence reports the question?

options.text: The journalist asked where were the sick pupils then.
The journalist asked where the sick pupils were then.
The journalist asked that where the sick pupils were then.
The journalist asked where the sick pupils are then.

questions.explanation: A reported question stops being a question: the subject goes back in front of its verb, so "where are the sick pupils" becomes "where the sick pupils were", and now becomes then. Keeping the inversion is the commonest mistake in the whole chapter; putting "that" in front of a question word is never possible in English; and leaving the verb in the present clashes with the past reporting verb asked.

questions.prompt: Complete: "After three weeks shut in at home, the children were ___ and their parents found the whole situation ___."
questions.explanation: An adjective in -ed says how somebody feels, an adjective in -ing says what causes the feeling. The children feel it, so they are depressed; the situation causes it, so it is depressing. Swapping the two turns the children into the cause and the situation into the sufferer; "depressive" is a medical word describing an illness or a character, not an ordinary mood; and calling the situation depressed leaves nobody actually feeling anything.
